name: Victor Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Victor. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. It's all confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. What's a normal day at work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Oakbrook Farm for the Mendes family: six hundred ewes, a hundred acres of wheat and an old apple orchard. Right now it's pruning in the orchard and checking the ewes before tupping, which is when the rams go in. In spring it's lambing, and that's three weeks of nights in the shed with a head torch. I've been there just over two years, so Paulo still double-checks my fences.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lambing, even the nights, when a weak lamb finally stands up. What wears me down is the money side. My partner Ana is a teaching assistant at the primary school, and we're saving for a house deposit while the rent keeps going up. We've got about five months of costs put away, which feels like a lot until you look at house prices.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. I ask a chatbot when a ewe looks wrong and the vet's not answering, and I check it with Paulo after. Clara, Paulo's daughter, uses it far more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, like most things. I'd say it to the lads at the pub quiz and leave it there. Online I'd maybe share a funny post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job's safe and the plan stays the same. Oakbrook is doing alright, Paulo isn't cutting anyone, and lamb prices were decent this year. The only thing bothering me is the house. Every year Ana and I save for a house deposit, the house prices go up again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Oakbrook and keep learning from Paulo, especially the shearing. We'd keep putting two hundred a month into the deposit pot. Maybe I'd ask about a small pay rise after lambing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. A bit frustrating about the house, but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the house prices keep going up. How far off is the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, about four years at this rate, if nothing goes wrong. Ana's mum has offered to help a bit. Ana doesn't want to take it, and I don't blame her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Paulo for that pay rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, after lambing, when he's seen what I can do. Paulo respects people who wait for the right moment. Asking in November would just get me a laugh.

say: I'd say it at the **pub quiz** and maybe share a **funny post**.

The **house deposit** is the only thing that bothers me.

Ana's pride about **family help** comes up without prompting.

steps.text: Learn shearing from Paulo at Oakbrook this season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and change on farms is nothing new, so we'll get on with it. At work I'd tell Clara I'm happy to try new kit once she's ironed it out. I wouldn't post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the thinking side lands on Clara, not me. She does the ordering, the paperwork, the lamb sales, and the AI would take most of that. My work is ewes, fences and pruning, and robots come slowly there. The bit I'd watch is Ana's school, because the AI marking and planning could mean fewer assistants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let Clara test the AI flock tools first, then learn them myself in the second season. We'd bump the deposit savings to two hundred and fifty, just in case Ana's hours drop. And I'd keep doing my job well, because a good worker is the last to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels a bit unsettled. Not for me exactly, more for Ana.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana if the school cut assistant hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ana we'd push the house back a year, not cancel it. She'd be upset, because she's great with the kids who struggle to read. A computer can't sit next to a seven-year-old who's crying over a book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a good worker is the last to go. Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. Paulo kept on old Teo for years after he slowed down, because Teo never missed a day. I know the market doesn't care, but Paulo does, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast and the government needs to slow it or cushion it. I'd say that in the pub and maybe in a comment online. I'd try not to sound panicked, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me. In 2028 the AI does everything Clara does in the office, and then around 2031 a robot can check ewes, fix fences and prune trees. Paulo might hold on to me for a while, but if robots are cheaper, Oakbrook can't afford not to buy them. And Ana's school job could go in 2028 already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the house hunt, because a mortgage now would be mad. I'd keep the deposit money as a safety cushion instead, five months plus whatever we add. I'd learn the AI tools Clara brings in straight away this time, not in year two. Then I'd watch for a year to see which farm jobs survive before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the plan I built just fell over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would hurt more, losing the house plan or losing Oakbrook?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Losing the house plan, oddly. I've known for a while farm work might not last forever. But the house was the thing Ana and I talked about every Sunday walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch for a year. With robots in three years, is a year of watching too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I don't want to jump into some course that's gone too by 2031. I'd rather watch for one year and then pick something I'm sure of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people are sensible. I'd say farmers should be thinking now about what they'll need people for. I'd keep it calm, like I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the same worry, slower. The AI comes in 2031 and takes Clara's side, and the robots arrive around 2034, when I'm thirty-five. I think Oakbrook keeps me till then, maybe longer because Paulo is old-fashioned. But I'd need a second skill by the time the robots come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a sheep-scanning course next year, because scanning ewes for lambs is skilled work farms pay well for. I'd keep saving for the deposit but aim for a smaller house, maybe a terrace in the village, in two years. And I'd learn the AI tools once Clara's tried them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable but tight. Like lambing when you know the weather's turning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Won't robots scan ewes too by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. But in the years before that, scanning pays three times a farm wage per day. If I scan for six seasons, that money is the house and a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a smaller house, sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a small house we own is safer than a nice house we can't get. Ana agrees, after a long talk. We'd rather have a roof that's ours by 2029 than wait for prices that never come down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if you use it. I'd tell the younger lads at Oakbrook to pick up a second skill. That's the sensible message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel okay about it. The AI comes in 2036 and the robots around 2039, when I'm forty. By then I want a house, maybe kids, and a skill people still pay for. Ten years is enough for all three if I don't sit on my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Oakbrook and save for the deposit as planned, buying in three or four years. I'd learn sheep scanning in the next two years and do it on the side in spring. And I'd learn the AI flock tools when Clara has them working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, with a bit of a nudge to get on with things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own kids about farm work, if you had them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my kids to love the land but not to count on it for a wage. Learn something with people in it. That's what my dad told me about the factory, and he was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you less worried about Ana's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. The school has time to change slowly, and Ana's thinking of training as a full teacher. If she does, she's the safer earner, and I'm fine with that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Ana's job and mine could both go before we own anything. What would help is help with housing for young couples, and short, paid courses for skills that will actually last. I'd also like employers to say plainly what they plan to buy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about owning things. If you own your house, you can survive a bad few years. If you rent, a bad year can end you.

headlineQuote: If you own your house, you can survive a bad few years.
portrait: Victor is a **27-year-old** junior shepherd and orchard hand at **Oakbrook Farm**.
He's **patient and practical**, and adopts AI tools after others prove them.
He and Ana are saving for a **house deposit**, his main goal in every picture.
He worries about **Ana's school job** as much as his own.
Faster AGI makes him **anxious**; with ten years he plans scanning and a house.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both jobs could go before they own a **home**.
whatWouldHelp: **Housing help** for young couples and short paid **courses**.
Plain **notice** from employers about what they plan to buy.
